claims.claim: Around AD 216 the Baths of Caracalla were Rome's largest public baths (the later Baths of Diocletian, about AD 306, became bigger).
claims.note: The video is set in AD 216, so 'biggest' is true for that moment. On screen: the hook headline "Rome's biggest bathhouse".

claims.claim: The Baths of Caracalla were built about AD 212–216 and opened around AD 216.
claims.note: Sources give completion as 216 or 216/217, so the script says 'around'.

claims.claim: Entry to Roman public baths usually cost a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin (and was sometimes free).
claims.note: General Roman practice, not a recorded price list for Caracalla's baths; said as 'one tiny coin'.

claims.claim: The Baths of Caracalla could hold about 1,600 bathers at once.
Bathers moved between a warm room (tepidarium), a hot room (caldarium) and a cold pool (frigidarium/natatio).
claims.note: The order varied by person and bath; the script gives one common route.

claims.claim: Hot rooms were heated by a hypocaust: furnace fires sending hot air under raised floors.
The main cold hall (frigidarium) was roofed by vaults about 32.9 metres high.
The Baths of Caracalla complex included public libraries.
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baths_of_Caracalla (libraries in the east and west exedrae)

claims.claim: Romans did not use soap at the baths; they rubbed olive oil on the skin and scraped it off with a curved metal strigil.
The bath furnaces were tended by enslaved workers.
The complex had exercise courts (palaestrae) as well as baths and libraries — a gym, spa and library in one.
claims.note: The ratings (5/5, 1/5) are Tilly's opinion, not claims.
